title: Muhammad Ali dynasty
capsule: Muhammad Ali Pasha, an Ottoman Albanian commander, seized control of Egypt in 1805 after the chaos left by Napoleon's 1798 invasion and was recognized as viceroy (wali) by the Porte. He modernized the Egyptian military and administration, destroyed the Mamluk power base in the Cairo Citadel massacre of 1811, and built a state monopoly economy that funded campaigns into Arabia (defeating the Wahhabi-Saudi state in 1818), Sudan (conquered 1820–1822), and Greece. His son Ibrahim Pasha's campaigns against the Ottomans (1831–1833, 1839–1840) brought Syria under Egyptian control and threatened Istanbul, prompting European intervention; the Convention of London (1840) forced Egypt's withdrawal to the Nile valley. The dynasty retained formal hereditary rule under Ottoman suzerainty through Muhammad Ali's successors until the khedival period that followed in 1866, with the dataset's geometry running to 1865.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Egypt proper under the dynasty is cartographically well-attested through Ottoman administrative records and 19th-century European surveys; the brief Syrian and Arabian occupations (1831–1840 and 1811–1818 respectively) are documented but the exact extent of administrative control in peripheral areas is imprecise.
